extracted.intended_audience: general educated readers; students/scholars of moral philosophy and Renaissance literature
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and normative observations relevant to composing and judging personal/philosophical essays and conduct: on intention, speech, idleness, truthfulness, prophecy, constancy, and honorable behaviour. Emphases are practical-maxims illustrated by historical examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intention is the judge of our actions
rubrics_metrics.description: The moral worth of actions is determined by the will and intention rather than by external outcomes or effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne argues we are masters only of our will and not of outcomes; examples include Henry VII’s posthumous order to execute the Duke of Suffolk and Count Egmont’s relying on death to discharge a promise. Where the will was sincere but performance impossible, the agent is absolved; where a man willfully and premeditatedly breaks faith (even postponing the wrong to after death), he is not excused. Surrounding commentary distinguishes obligations tied to capacity and the timing of restitution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Death does not automatically absolve deliberate bad faith
rubrics_metrics.description: One cannot hide a deliberately premeditated breach of faith behind death — death does not absolve intentionally planned wrongdoing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by Henry VII who ordered an execution to occur after his death and by Count Egmont’s case; Montaigne stresses the difference between inability and willful design. Practical takeaway: moral assessment looks to prior intention and planning rather than mere fact of death.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make restitution promptly; penitence requires penalty
rubrics_metrics.description: Attempting to make amends only in a will or at death is less just and less meritorious than timely restitution, and those who delay lessen the value of their reparations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne criticises those who try to correct unjust detention of another’s goods by will alone or who reserve animosity until death. He notes restitution should be strict and costly to the self to be truly meritorious; delaying repair diminishes moral worth and aggravates injury to the offended party.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivate the mind; avoid idleness
rubrics_metrics.description: An uncultivated, idle mind wanders into unproductive, fantastical, or harmful imaginings; mental leisure must be guided by study and application to bear useful fruit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne compares untilled ground producing weeds to a mind left unrestrained producing chimaeras. He advises fixing minds with a study or aim that restrains imagination, and to 'husband' leisure so it yields ordered, profitable thoughts rather than extravagant fancies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leisure alone breeds varied and disorderly thought
rubrics_metrics.description: Leisure by itself tends to produce a multiplicity of random, disordered ideas rather than measured reflection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quotations and examples stress that leisure 'ever creates varied thought' and that absence of an established aim causes the soul to 'lose itself.' Montaigne records his own experience: absolute leisure led to extravagant fancies that he began to set to paper to shame them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value truth; lying is an accursed vice
rubrics_metrics.description: Lying (deliberately asserting what one knows to be false) is morally corrupting, socially destructive, and should be severely checked from early age.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes between honest error (untruth believed true) and conscious lying. Montaigne asserts liars are self-ensnaring — contradictory versions and the persistence of true impressions expose falsehoods. He condemns permissive parental treatment of lying and recommends strict correction; gives diplomatic examples of reputational ruin caused by falsehood (ambassadors tripped by their lies). The social fabric depends on truthfulness ('we are not men... but by our word').

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not practice lying if you lack memory
rubrics_metrics.description: Those without good memory should especially avoid lying, since maintaining falsehoods requires remembering numerous invented details liable to contradiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne notes that liars who invent different colours of a story for different audiences will inevitably be trapped when accounts are compared; a weak memory both reduces capacity for deceit and curbs dangerous ambition and loquacity. This is offered as both practical counsel and ironic consolation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match speech tempo to role; favour natural promptness
rubrics_metrics.description: The appropriateness of quick (extempore) versus slow (premeditated) speech depends on context — quick speech suits the bar and debate, slow suits the pulpit — and over-labouring a speech can strip it of grace.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne advises fitting the speaker’s tempo to their function: pleaders need to respond extempore to objections, preachers may use slow, deliberate composition. He cautions against over-elaboration ('stink of oil and of the lamp'), since forced, overstrained composition loses vivacity; accident, occasion and company often draw out better speech than solitary premeditation. Examples: Poyet failing to adapt a prepared harangue at Marseilles; Severus Cassius excelling extempore.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be skeptical of prognostications and divination
rubrics_metrics.description: Oracles, auguries, star-readings, dreams and other prognostications are unreliable guides for action and decision; occasional accurate hits arise from chance and confirmers record only successes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne surveys the decay of oracles and mocks reliance on divination (flight of birds, entrails, dreams). He adduces historical episodes of rulers misled, notes that ambiguous prophetic cant is designed so authors can later retro-fit meanings, and observes humans tend to record hits and forget misses (Diogenes example). Practical guidance: do not base policy or private enterprise on such vanities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constancy is resolute endurance coupled with prudent precaution
rubrics_metrics.description: True constancy does not mean reckless exposure to harm nor the absence of fear; it means bravely standing to and stoutly suffering harms that cannot be avoided while using decent means to secure oneself from mischiefs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne clarifies that resolution permits and commends reasonable measures to avoid harms; constancy’s chief business is to endure unavoidable inconveniences. The entry marks a balance between courage and prudence rather than blind stoicism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Honour in victory: avoid treachery and unfair advantage
rubrics_metrics.description: There is moral superiority in obtaining victory by fair means (valour or wisdom) rather than by treachery, ambush, or deceitful stratagems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne contrasts Ariosto's praise of victory by fortune or wit with Chrysippus and Alexander’s forbidding of treacherous night attacks. Historical examples (sieges where defenders were captured while parleying) show the moral distaste and practical consequences of 'stealing a victory.' He privileges honourable conduct in conflict even when stratagems might secure success.
